subject: System Design — Case Studies
summary: System design case studies are the interview format where a one-line prompt — 'design WhatsApp' — must become a scoped, sized, justified architecture in 45 minutes. Companies test it because it predicts the real job better than any coding puzzle: can you clarify requirements, do honest capacity math, choose storage by access pattern, and defend trade-offs with numbers instead of buzzwords? This subject walks nine canonical cases (URL shortener, rate limiter, chat, news feed, typeahead, notifications, job scheduler, ride-hailing, video) through one fixed template: requirements with numbers, worked estimates, API, data model, diagram, the deep dive the interviewer will pick, then bottlenecks and follow-ups. Study it by rehearsing the template out loud per case until the estimate arithmetic (86,400 seconds/day, the latency ladder, read:write ratios) is automatic — the cross-cutting judgment questions at the end are where offers are actually decided.

sections.title: 1. The 45-Minute Template: How Every Case Study Runs
sections.content:
Start with why a template exists at all. A system design interview is not a trivia quiz about what Netflix uses — the interviewer is testing whether you can take a vague one-line prompt ("design WhatsApp") and turn it into a scoped, sized, justified design under time pressure. Candidates fail this round in two ways: they jump straight to drawing boxes without agreeing on what the system must do, or they spend thirty minutes on requirements and never design anything. A fixed template protects you from both.

Every case study on this site follows the same eight steps, and you should run them in this order out loud:

```
 minutes   step
 0-5       Requirements  — functional (what it does) and
                           non-functional (how well: QPS, latency, durability)
 5-10      Estimates     — worked math: QPS, storage, bandwidth, connections
 10-13     API sketch    — 3-6 endpoints, request/response shapes
 13-17     Data model    — tables/keys, and WHICH database shape and why
 17-27     High-level    — one diagram, walk a request through it end to end
 27-40     Deep dive     — the ONE hard sub-problem, in detail
 40-45     Bottlenecks   — what breaks first at 10x, and follow-up questions
```

The estimates step is where most candidates stall, so memorize the arithmetic shortcuts. A day is 86,400 seconds — round it to 10^5. So 1 million requests per day is about 12 per second; 100 million per day is about 1,200 per second; 1 billion per day is about 12,000 per second. Peak traffic is 2-3x the average unless the product is bursty (ticket sales, live events), where it can be 10x. For storage, count bytes per record, multiply by records per day, then by retention: 1 KB per record at 10 million records per day is 10 GB per day, about 3.6 TB per year.

You also need the latency ladder, because it justifies every cache you add: a main-memory read is ~100 nanoseconds, an SSD random read ~100 microseconds, a disk seek ~10 milliseconds, a round trip inside one datacenter ~0.5 milliseconds, and a round trip across an ocean ~150 milliseconds. That last number is why CDNs exist (a CDN is a fleet of edge servers near users that cache your content so requests never cross the ocean), and the first three are why "put it in Redis" is a real answer and not hand-waving: RAM beats disk by roughly 100x, and beats a cross-region hop by 1,000x.

Two habits separate strong candidates. First, state the read:write ratio early — almost every design decision (caching, fan-out direction, database choice) follows from whether the system is read-heavy (URL shortener, news feed: 100:1 or more) or write-heavy (chat, location tracking: near 1:1). Second, when you make a choice, name the alternative you rejected and the number that killed it: "I am precomputing feeds because reads outnumber writes 200 to 1, so paying at write time is 200x cheaper." When the interviewer hears a number attached to a decision, they check the judgment box. When they hear a technology name with no number, they start digging until they find the edge of your knowledge.

sections.title: 2. URL Shortener: The Canonical Opener
sections.content:
This is the most common warm-up because it looks trivial and is not. The interviewer is testing whether you can size a system honestly, pick a database for the right reason, and design an ID scheme — three skills every later case reuses.

REQUIREMENTS. Functional: given a long URL, return a short one; visiting the short URL redirects to the original; optional custom aliases ("bit.ly/my-launch"); optional expiry. Non-functional — and say these with numbers: 100 million new URLs per month, read:write ratio 100:1 (redirects vastly outnumber creations), redirect latency p99 under 100 ms because a slow redirect delays every page behind it, 99.9% availability, links kept for 5 years. Explicitly descope analytics dashboards and user accounts unless asked — descoping out loud is a skill being graded.

ESTIMATES. Writes: 100M per month / 2.6M seconds per month ≈ 40 URLs/s. Reads: 100x that ≈ 4,000/s average, 12,000/s peak. Storage: 100M/month × 60 months = 6 billion records; at ~500 bytes each (the long URL dominates) that is 3 TB total — small. Conclusion you should say out loud: this system is not storage-bound or write-bound; it is read-latency-bound. That single sentence drives the whole design.

Short code length: with base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9), 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations. 7 characters covers 6 billion URLs with 500x headroom.

API SKETCH.

```
POST /urls        {longUrl, customAlias?, expiresAt?} -> {shortUrl}
GET  /{code}      -> HTTP 302 redirect, Location: <longUrl>
DELETE /urls/{code}
```

DATA MODEL. One table: code (primary key), long_url, created_at, expires_at, owner_id. No joins, no transactions across rows, lookup is always by exact key. That access pattern is the textbook case for a key-value store (a database that only supports get/put by key, like DynamoDB or Redis-backed storage) — but say the honest version: at 3 TB and 12k reads/s, a single beefy Postgres with a read replica also works; you choose KV for operational headroom, not necessity.

HIGH-LEVEL.

```
 write:  client -> API -> ID generator -> DB
 read:   client -> LB -> API --(1) Redis cache: code -> longUrl
                            \--(2) on miss: DB, then fill cache
                    -> 302 redirect
```

DEEP DIVE: ID GENERATION — this is what the interviewer will pick. Option A: hash the long URL (MD5, take first 7 base62 chars). Problem: collisions (two URLs producing the same code) — at billions of rows they will happen, so you must check-and-reprobe, and the same URL from two users yields the same code, which breaks per-user expiry. Option B: a global auto-increment counter converted to base62. Clean and collision-free, but a single counter is a single point of failure and a write bottleneck. Fix: allocate ranges — each app server asks a coordinator (or a database row, or ZooKeeper) for a block of 100,000 IDs and hands them out from memory; a crashed server wastes at most one block, which is fine given 3.5 trillion of headroom. Option C: a Key Generation Service that pre-generates random unused codes into a pool. Ranges (Option B) is the answer most interviewers want to hear, with the caveat that sequential codes are guessable — competitors can walk your namespace and measure your volume — so you either randomize within blocks or accept it.

Second deep-dive magnet: 301 vs 302. A 301 (permanent redirect) gets cached by the browser, so repeat visits never hit your servers — cheaper, but you lose all click data and cannot change or expire the mapping for that user. A 302 (temporary) keeps every click on your servers. A link service whose business is analytics must use 302; say the trade-off, then choose.

BOTTLENECKS AND EVOLUTION. First thing to break: a hot link (a celebrity tweets it) sends 100k reads/s at one key. The Redis cache absorbs this — cache the top ~20M codes (about 10 GB) and hot links are served without touching the DB; put a CDN in front if one link can go globally viral. Next: analytics. Never increment a click counter synchronously on the redirect path; emit an event to a queue and count asynchronously, keeping the redirect at one cache read. Growth path: when one DB node is not enough, shard by code — the code is random, so load spreads evenly, and every read names its shard.

FOLLOW-UPS THEY WILL ASK: how do you clean up expired links (lazy delete on read plus a nightly sweep — never a giant synchronous purge); how do you stop abuse (rate-limit creation per API key, scan destinations against a malware blocklist asynchronously); what if two requests claim the same custom alias (unique constraint in the DB, first writer wins, second gets 409); why not UUIDs (128 bits is 22 base62 chars — defeats the purpose of being short).

sections.title: 3. Rate Limiter as a Service
sections.content:
Why a service and not a library? Because when forty microservices each implement their own throttling, the rules drift: the mobile gateway allows 100 requests/min, the web gateway 60, and nobody can answer "what limits does customer X actually have?" Centralizing rate limiting into one service gives one rule store, one place to change limits during an incident, and consistent counting when a user's requests land on different gateways. The cost is a network hop on every request — the whole design is about making that hop cheap and survivable.

REQUIREMENTS. Functional: limit by API key, user ID, or IP; multiple rules per key (e.g. 10/s AND 10,000/day); on rejection return 429 with a Retry-After header so clients back off instead of hammering. Non-functional: the check must add under 2 ms p99 (it sits on every request in the company), handle 100,000 checks/s, and have an explicit failure policy — if the limiter is down, do gateways allow traffic (fail-open) or block it (fail-closed)? Fail-open for product endpoints (an outage should not take down the site), fail-closed for abuse-sensitive ones like login and OTP (a limiter outage must not become a free brute-force window). Saying that pair unprompted is a strong signal.

ESTIMATES. 100k checks/s against counter state: 10M active keys × 3 rules × ~100 bytes of counter state ≈ 3 GB — fits comfortably in a small Redis cluster. A single Redis node does ~100k ops/s, so 2-4 shards give headroom. The state is small; the problem is latency and atomicity, not size.

ALGORITHMS — know all four, recommend one. Fixed window (count per calendar minute) is cheapest but allows 2x bursts at boundaries: 100 requests at 11:59:59 and 100 more at 12:00:01 both pass a 100/min limit. Sliding window log stores a timestamp per request — exact, but 10,000 requests/day per key is 10,000 timestamps of memory each. Sliding window counter blends the previous and current fixed windows weighted by overlap — a good accuracy/memory compromise. Token bucket is the usual recommendation: a bucket holds up to `capacity` tokens, refilled at `rate` per second; each request spends one token; an empty bucket means 429. It permits short bursts up to capacity (good for real clients, which are bursty) while capping the sustained rate, and its state is two numbers per key: token count and last-refill time.

```
 client -> API gateway --(check key, cost)--> limiter svc -> Redis shard
                        <-- allow / deny+Retry-After --     (Lua script,
             on allow: forward to backend                    atomic)
```

DEEP DIVE: ATOMICITY — the interviewer will pick this. The naive flow is read counter, compare, write counter+1. With two gateways doing this concurrently you get a race condition (two readers both see 9 under a limit of 10, both allow, the true count becomes 11). The fix in Redis is a Lua script: Redis executes a script as one atomic unit, so read-refill-compare-decrement happens with no interleaving. Alternative fix: INCR first and check the returned value, undoing if over — atomic but chattier. Shard by key so all counters for one key live on one shard — cross-shard counting would need coordination you do not want on the hot path.

Latency trick worth naming: give each gateway a local in-memory token bucket for coarse limits and consult Redis only every N requests or for strict rules. You trade exactness (a key can briefly exceed its limit by the sum of local allowances) for removing the network hop from most requests. Strict correctness for billing-grade limits, local approximation for abuse protection — name which rule gets which.

BOTTLENECKS AND EVOLUTION. Hot key: one huge customer sends 50k req/s and all their counters sit on one Redis shard. Split that key's counter into K sub-counters on different shards, sum approximately, accept a few percent of error. Multi-region: a global limit of 1,000/s across three regions either needs cross-region sync on every request (dead on arrival: 150 ms hops) or per-region budgets (334/s each) rebalanced asynchronously every few seconds — pick the second, say the word "approximate" proudly. Rule changes: push rules to limiter nodes via config service with versioning; never make gateways fetch rules per request.

FOLLOW-UPS THEY WILL ASK: how does the client know when to retry (Retry-After plus jittered exponential backoff — jitter prevents synchronized retry storms); should a rejected request cost a token (no — otherwise a throttled client can never recover); how do you rate limit by cost, not count (spend N tokens for expensive endpoints); how do you test limits in production without hurting users (shadow mode: compute the decision, log it, do not enforce, compare against expected volumes).

import time

class TokenBucket:
    # Token bucket: allows bursts up to `capacity`, sustained rate `rate`/sec.
    # State per key is two numbers: tokens and last-refill timestamp.
    def __init__(self, rate, capacity, now=None):
        self.rate = float(rate)
        self.capacity = float(capacity)
        self.tokens = float(capacity)
        self.last = now if now is not None else time.monotonic()

    def allow(self, now=None, cost=1.0):
        now = now if now is not None else time.monotonic()
        # refill proportionally to elapsed time, capped at capacity
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost
            return True
        return False

# rate 5/s, burst capacity 10, driven by a fake clock for determinism
b = TokenBucket(rate=5, capacity=10, now=0.0)

# burst: exactly 10 immediate requests pass, the 11th is rejected
results = [b.allow(now=0.0) for _ in range(11)]
assert results == [True] * 10 + [False]

# after 1 second, 5 tokens refilled -> 5 pass, 6th rejected
results = [b.allow(now=1.0) for _ in range(6)]
assert results == [True] * 5 + [False]

# long idle does NOT bank more than capacity
b2 = TokenBucket(rate=5, capacity=10, now=0.0)
b2.allow(now=100.0)  # refill capped at 10, spend 1 -> 9 left
assert abs(b2.tokens - 9.0) < 1e-9

print("token bucket ok: burst capped at capacity, sustained rate enforced")

sections.title: 4. Chat / WhatsApp: Fan-Out, Presence, and Ordering
sections.content:
Chat flips the shape of every system before it: it is write-heavy, latency is felt in hundreds of milliseconds by two humans staring at the same conversation, and the server must PUSH data to clients instead of waiting to be asked. The interviewer is testing whether you know how push works at scale and whether you can reason about ordering and delivery guarantees — the two places where chat designs quietly go wrong.

REQUIREMENTS. Functional: 1:1 chat and groups up to 500 members; delivery states (sent / delivered / read); online presence (who is online now); message history on any device. Non-functional: 50M daily active users each sending ~40 messages/day; end-to-end delivery under 500 ms p99 when both users are online; messages never lost once the server acks them (at-least-once delivery — the server may deliver a message twice but never zero times); per-conversation ordering (messages appear in the same order for everyone).

ESTIMATES. 50M × 40 = 2B messages/day ≈ 23,000/s average, ~70,000/s peak. Storage: ~300 bytes per message with metadata → 600 GB/day → roughly 1 PB over 5 years, so history lives in a horizontally scalable store from day one. Connections: assume 25% of DAU online at peak = 12.5M concurrent sockets. A tuned server holds ~250k WebSocket connections (a WebSocket is a persistent bidirectional TCP connection kept open so the server can push instantly), so ~50 gateway boxes. HTTP polling instead would mean 12.5M clients asking "anything new?" every 2 seconds — 6M QPS of mostly-empty responses; that comparison is why WebSockets, and reciting it earns points.

HIGH-LEVEL.

```
 sender app ==ws== gateway A -> chat service -> msg store (Cassandra)
                                    |             (write first, then deliver)
                                    v
                          session registry (Redis: user -> gateway)
                                    |
 recipient app ==ws== gateway B <---+   offline? -> push notification svc
```

The session registry is the piece candidates forget: with 50 gateways, the chat service must know WHICH gateway holds the recipient's socket. Keep a Redis map user_id → gateway_id, written on connect, expired by heartbeat. Persist the message BEFORE attempting delivery — durability first, so a gateway crash mid-delivery loses nothing; the client re-fetches on reconnect from its last acknowledged position (a cursor: the ID of the newest message the device has confirmed).

API SKETCH. Over the socket: send {clientMsgId, convId, text}, ack {msgId}, receipt {msgId, state}. Over plain HTTP: GET /conversations/{id}/messages?before=cursor for history, because history is a normal paged read and does not need the socket.

DATA MODEL. Messages: partition key conversation_id, clustering key message_id descending — one conversation's messages live together, newest first, which matches the only real query ("latest N messages in this chat"). This is the canonical wide-column-store shape (Cassandra/Scylla: high write throughput, partition-local ordering, no cross-row transactions — none needed here).

DEEP DIVE: ORDERING AND DEDUPLICATION — the interviewer will pick this. Wall-clock timestamps cannot order messages: clock skew (two servers' clocks disagreeing, routinely by milliseconds) means B's reply can carry an earlier timestamp than A's question. Instead, route each conversation to one owning shard of the chat service (consistent hash on conversation_id) and let that owner assign a per-conversation monotonically increasing sequence number. One writer per conversation makes ordering a local, straightforwardly correct operation; the cost is that a hot 500-member group is capped by one shard's throughput, which is fine — one group producing thousands of messages per second is not a real workload. For delivery: transport is at-least-once (retry until ack), so clients may receive duplicates; the client generates a UUID per message (clientMsgId) and both server and client deduplicate on it. At-least-once transport plus idempotent storage looks exactly-once to users — that sentence is the answer to "how do you guarantee exactly-once?", because true exactly-once transport over a network that can fail is impossible.

PRESENCE. Naive presence is a fan-out bomb: if every connect/disconnect is pushed to all contacts, 12.5M users × ~200 contacts of events at commute time melts the system. Do it lazily: heartbeat every 20 s updates last_seen; clients PULL presence only for the conversation list currently on screen, and subscribe to live updates only for the open chat. Presence may lag ~30 s; nobody notices, and say so.

BOTTLENECKS AND EVOLUTION. Gateway death: 250k clients reconnect at once — a thundering herd (many clients retrying simultaneously, creating the very overload they are retrying around); clients must use jittered exponential backoff, and gateways shed load by accepting connections gradually. Groups: write the message once, fan out delivery pointers to ≤500 members via the registry; the 500 cap exists precisely to bound this fan-out. Multi-device: each device keeps its own cursor; the server delivers to every registered device independently.

FOLLOW-UPS THEY WILL ASK: end-to-end encryption (server stores ciphertext; server-side search and abuse scanning become impossible — features move client-side); media (never through the socket — upload to blob storage, send the URL as a message); read receipts at scale (they are messages too, same pipeline, but batch them); what if the session registry is stale (delivery to a dead gateway fails, fall back to push notification and correct the registry).

sections.title: 5. News Feed: Push vs Pull Fan-Out Economics
sections.content:
The news feed question has one real center: when a user posts, do you deliver that post to followers now (at write time) or when they ask (at read time)? Everything else — storage, caching, ranking — hangs off that choice. The interviewer is testing whether you can do the cost arithmetic for both and land on the hybrid, because the pure versions each fail at a specific, computable point.

REQUIREMENTS. Functional: follow users; create posts; read a feed of recent posts from people you follow, newest-first (rank later). Non-functional: 200M DAU; each opens the feed ~10 times/day; 10M new posts/day; median user has 200 followers; celebrities reach 100M; feed must load in under 500 ms p99; a slightly stale feed (missing the last minute) is acceptable — say that, it is the relaxation that makes the design possible; your OWN post must appear in your feed immediately.

ESTIMATES. Feed reads: 200M × 10 = 2B/day ≈ 23,000/s. Post writes: 10M/day ≈ 116/s. Read:write is roughly 200:1 — this system exists to serve reads.

PUSH (fan-out on write): when a user posts, insert the post ID into a precomputed per-follower feed list. Cost: 10M posts × 200 median followers = 2B list inserts/day ≈ 23,000/s — cheap Redis LPUSH operations, entirely affordable. Reads become one list fetch: fast, and this is why push is the default. The failure case: one celebrity post to 100M followers = 100M inserts. At 100k inserts/s across the fan-out fleet, that single post takes ~17 minutes to deliver, and a news event where ten celebrities post burns hours of fan-out capacity delivering to mostly-idle accounts.

PULL (fan-out on read): store posts once; when a user opens the feed, fetch recent posts from each of their ~200 followees and merge. Cost: 2B feed loads × 200 lookups = 400B reads/day ≈ 4.6M reads/s. Even with aggressive caching of per-author recent-post lists, you are paying 200x per read to avoid a 1x write — backwards for a 200:1 read-heavy system. Pull only wins for authors whose follower count makes push explode.

HYBRID — the answer: push for everyone under a follower threshold (say 100k), pull for accounts above it. At read time: fetch the user's precomputed list, fetch recent posts from the handful of celebrities they follow (heavily cached — a million fans requesting one celebrity's recent posts is one cache key), merge, return. A typical user follows a few celebrities, so the merge is a ~5-way, not 200-way, operation.

```
 post (normal user) -> post svc -> posts DB
                          \-> fanout queue -> workers -> follower feed
                                                          lists (Redis)
 post (celebrity)   -> posts DB only (no fan-out)

 read feed -> feed svc -> own list (Redis)  --+
                       -> celeb recent posts -+-> merge -> hydrate -> rank
                          (shared cache)
```

DATA MODEL. follows(follower_id, followee_id) — you need BOTH directions ("whom do I follow" to build feeds on read, "who follows me" to fan out on write), which on a sharded store means two tables or a covering index, one keyed each way. posts(post_id, author_id, content, created_at) with post_id a Snowflake-style ID (64 bits: timestamp + machine + sequence) so IDs sort by creation time — that makes "newest first" a sort by ID and gives you cursor pagination for free. Feed lists: Redis list per user, capped at ~300 post IDs (IDs only — hydrate content from a post cache at read time; storing full posts per follower would multiply storage by the follower count). Memory: 200M users × 300 × 16 bytes ≈ 1 TB across the cluster — real but routine.

DEEP DIVE the interviewer will pick: the fan-out worker path. Posts go onto a queue (a buffer between producer and consumers so a burst of posts does not require instant fan-out capacity); workers read follower lists in chunks of 10k and LPUSH+LTRIM each follower's list. Skip followers inactive for 30+ days — fanning out to dead accounts is pure waste, often more than half of it; rebuild a returning user's feed via one pull-mode query. This inactivity optimization is a favorite "how would you cut this cost 50%?" answer.

BOTTLENECKS AND EVOLUTION. Read-your-writes (you post, refresh, and your post must be there): insert into the author's OWN feed list synchronously before the async fan-out, or union your own recent posts at read time. Deletes and edits: the post ID is already in a million lists you cannot efficiently visit — filter at read time against a tombstone set (deleted-post IDs), and let capped lists age the ID out naturally. Ranking: fetch ~500 candidate IDs by recency, hydrate, score with a separate ML service, return top 50 — candidate generation and ranking are separate tiers, and naming that split reads as senior.

FOLLOW-UPS THEY WILL ASK: what threshold splits push from pull (wherever fan-out lag exceeds your freshness budget — compute it: at 100k inserts/s fleet capacity, 100k followers ≈ 1 s of lag, 10M ≈ 100 s; pick the follower count where lag breaks the product, and note the real constraint is total daily fan-out volume, so the threshold is tuned empirically); how do ads and injected content enter (at the merge/rank step, never fanned out); what breaks at 10x DAU (feed-list memory and fan-out volume scale linearly — shard Redis further, tighten the inactivity cutoff, lower the celebrity threshold).

sections.title: 6. Autocomplete / Typeahead: Trie + Top-K
sections.content:
Typeahead looks small and is one of the highest-QPS systems a company runs, because every keystroke is a request. The interviewer is testing three things: whether you notice the QPS multiplier, whether you know why a trie with PRECOMPUTED top-k beats computing suggestions at query time, and whether you separate the serving path (read-only, in-memory, microseconds) from the build path (offline, batch, hours).

REQUIREMENTS. Functional: given a typed prefix, return the top 10 completions ranked by popularity; suggestions reflect trending queries within a few hours. Non-functional: 5B searches/day, and each search averages ~4 keystrokes that fire a request → 20B requests/day ≈ 230,000/s average, ~500,000/s peak. Latency under 100 ms p99 END TO END — the human perception budget for "instant" — which leaves single-digit milliseconds for the server. Staleness of hours is fine. That relaxation (reads are from a snapshot, updates are batch) is the load-bearing design decision.

WHY A TRIE, AND WHY PRECOMPUTED. A trie (prefix tree — one node per character path, so all completions of "ca" live under the c→a node) makes prefix lookup O(length of prefix). But the naive query — walk to the prefix node, then explore the whole subtree below it collecting completions and sorting by frequency — touches thousands of nodes for short prefixes ("t" has almost the whole corpus under it). At 500k QPS that is dead. The fix: at BUILD time, store at every node the already-ranked top 10 completions for that prefix. A query becomes: walk k character nodes, read one precomputed list. Microseconds. You pay with build-time work and memory — the correct trade for a 20B-read, batch-write workload. The DB alternative (SELECT ... WHERE query LIKE 'ca%' ORDER BY freq LIMIT 10) is worth naming: a B-tree index serves the prefix range scan fine, but re-sorting by frequency per request at this QPS is hopeless — LIKE-on-Postgres is the right answer only below a few thousand QPS.

ESTIMATES (memory). Keep the top ~100M distinct queries (frequency-thresholded — the long tail of one-off queries is noise). Raw text ≈ 100M × 25 bytes = 2.5 GB; trie nodes plus a top-10 list per node lands around 10-15 GB — fits in RAM on one 64 GB box. So sharding is driven by QPS, not size: at ~50k QPS per box you need ~10 replicas at peak. If the corpus were 10x bigger, shard by prefix — but hash the first 2-3 characters with a load-aware routing map, because raw alphabetical ranges are wildly uneven ("s" and "t" dwarf "x").

```
 build path (offline, hourly/daily):
   search logs -> aggregate counts (Spark) -> build trie + top-10 per node
              -> versioned snapshot -> push to serving fleet -> atomic swap

 serve path (online, per keystroke):
   client (with local cache) -> LB -> trie replica -> merge trending overlay
                                                    -> top 10
```

The atomic swap matters: serving nodes load the new snapshot alongside the old, then flip a pointer — never mutate a live trie under 500k QPS of readers. For freshness, layer a small "trending overlay" (last few hours of hot queries, rebuilt every few minutes) merged with the main snapshot at query time; full rebuild stays daily.

DATA MODEL is the trie itself — this system's "database" is a purpose-built in-memory index, and saying so is the point: not every store is Postgres or Redis; sometimes the data structure IS the design.

DEEP DIVE the interviewer will pick: maintaining top-k at build time. Build bottom-up: each node's top-10 is the merge of its children's top-10 lists plus its own terminal query — k-way merge of small sorted lists, O(alphabet × 10) per node, one pass over the trie. They may push: "why store only 10 — what if the UI wants 20?" Precompute the max the product will ever show; k is small precisely because humans read few suggestions.

BOTTLENECKS AND EVOLUTION. Hot prefixes: the first 1-2 keystrokes dominate traffic AND have the most static results — cache them hardest: client-side cache (the same user retypes "we" constantly), CDN/edge cache with a 1-hour TTL for 1-2 char prefixes. This can shed half the backend load, and it is the follow-up answer they are fishing for with "500k QPS is expensive — reduce it." Debounce on the client (wait ~50 ms of typing pause before firing) cuts another chunk. Filtering: profanity/abuse blocklists applied at build time, plus a fast deny-set at serve time for emergency removals — you cannot wait a day for a rebuild when legal calls.

FOLLOW-UPS THEY WILL ASK: personalization (blend a small per-user history — client-side or a tiny per-user store — with global results at merge time; do not build per-user tries); typo tolerance (fuzzy matching explores sibling branches within edit distance 1 — costs latency, gate it to longer prefixes); multi-language (separate tries per language/market — sharding by market is also the natural deployment split); why not Elasticsearch (its edge-ngram feature does exactly this and is the right call at startup scale; the custom trie earns its complexity only past tens of thousands of QPS).
