import heapq

class TrieNode:
    __slots__ = ("children", "top", "freq")
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.top = []      # precomputed [(freq, query)] best-first, len <= K
        self.freq = 0      # frequency if a query terminates here, else 0

K = 3  # top-k per node (10 in prod; 3 here to keep the demo readable)

def build(corpus):
    root = TrieNode()
    for query, freq in corpus.items():
        node = root
        for ch in query:
            node = node.children.setdefault(ch, TrieNode())
        node.freq = freq
    _precompute(root, "")
    return root

def _precompute(node, prefix):
    # bottom-up: my top-k = merge of children's top-k + my own terminal query
    candidates = []
    if node.freq:
        candidates.append((node.freq, prefix))
    for ch, child in node.children.items():
        _precompute(child, prefix + ch)
        candidates.extend(child.top)
    # nlargest of a few small lists: cheap, done once at build time
    node.top = heapq.nlargest(K, candidates)

def suggest(root, prefix):
    node = root
    for ch in prefix:          # O(len(prefix)) walk...
        if ch not in node.children:
            return []
        node = node.children[ch]
    return [q for _, q in node.top]  # ...then ONE precomputed list read

corpus = {"cat": 100, "car": 90, "card": 80, "care": 40, "dog": 70, "cart": 10}
root = build(corpus)

assert suggest(root, "ca") == ["cat", "car", "card"]   # ranked by frequency
assert suggest(root, "car") == ["car", "card", "care"] # "cart" loses: k=3 cutoff
assert suggest(root, "d") == ["dog"]
assert suggest(root, "zz") == []
print("trie top-k ok: query cost = prefix walk + one list read")

sections.title: 7. Notification System: Channels, Queues, and Idempotency
sections.content:
Every product team eventually needs to send users messages — order shipped, password OTP, marketing blast — and if each team calls Apple/Google/Twilio directly, you get duplicated retry logic, no unified opt-out handling, and one team's campaign exhausting the SMS budget of another. A notification system is the internal service that owns "deliver this message to this user on the right channel, once." The interviewer is testing whether you design around the two facts that define this domain: external providers are slow and flaky, and duplicates are unacceptable in a world where retries are mandatory.

REQUIREMENTS. Functional: four channels — mobile push (via APNs for iOS, FCM for Android — the platform gateways you MUST go through), email, SMS, in-app; triggered by internal services via API or by events; templating (one template, per-user variables); user preferences and opt-outs honored per channel; delivery status tracking. Non-functional: 150M notifications/day ≈ 1,700/s average, but a 10M-recipient campaign that must drain in 30 minutes adds ~5,500/s of burst; OTP codes must arrive in under 5 seconds even DURING that campaign; no user gets the same notification twice; at-least-once handoff to providers with retries.

ESTIMATES. The math above already yields the key insight: average load is trivial, burst load is 4x average, and the latency-critical traffic (OTP) is a tiny fraction of volume. So the design problem is ISOLATION — keeping bulk traffic from starving urgent traffic — not raw throughput. Storage: a 1 KB log row per notification × 150M/day ≈ 150 GB/day, kept 90 days ≈ 13 TB — a partitioned log table, nothing exotic.

```
 producers (order svc, auth svc, marketing)
      -> notification API (validate, check prefs/opt-out, render template,
                           assign idempotency key)
      -> Kafka topics:  push.critical | push.bulk | email | sms | inapp
      -> channel workers (rate-limited per provider)
      -> APNs / FCM / SES / Twilio
      -> provider callbacks + worker results -> status store -> analytics
```

WHY QUEUES SIT IN THE MIDDLE. Providers throttle (APNs and Twilio both push back under load), fail transiently, and take 50-500 ms per call. A queue (a durable buffer that decouples producers from consumers) absorbs the campaign burst so producers return immediately, lets workers retry with exponential backoff without re-involving the producer, and — the isolation requirement — separate topics per channel AND per priority mean a Twilio slowdown queues SMS without delaying push, and OTPs ride a critical topic with its own dedicated workers that bulk traffic can never occupy. Putting OTP and marketing on one shared queue is the classic failure here; interviewers deliberately probe for it with "a campaign is running and a user requests a login code — walk me through what happens."

DATA MODEL. templates(id, channel, body); preferences(user_id, channel, opted_in, quiet_hours); device_tokens(user_id, token, platform, last_seen) — plural tokens per user, one per device, PRUNED when APNs/FCM report a token invalid (their feedback is how you learn a user deleted the app; ignoring it gets your sender reputation throttled); notification_log(idempotency_key, user_id, channel, status, timestamps).

DEEP DIVE the interviewer will pick: EXACTLY-ONCE, OR RATHER ITS IMPOSSIBILITY. If a worker sends to Twilio and crashes before recording success, did the SMS go out? Unknowable — so on restart you either re-send (possible duplicate) or drop (possible loss). Networks make exactly-once delivery to an external party impossible; what you build instead is at-least-once delivery plus deduplication: every notification carries an idempotency key (event_id + user_id + channel), and a worker claims it in Redis with SETNX and a TTL (SETNX = set-if-not-exists, atomic, so exactly one claimer wins) before calling the provider. A crash after claim but before send means that notification may be lost until the TTL expires and a retry reclaims it — you have converted "maybe duplicate" into "maybe delayed," which is the correct trade for everything except OTP, where a duplicate SMS is harmless and loss is not, so OTP workers claim AFTER a successful send. Showing you can flip the trade per traffic class is exactly the judgment being graded.

BOTTLENECKS AND EVOLUTION. Provider rate limits: a token bucket per provider connection keeps you inside contract limits; overflow waits in the queue, which is what it is for. Retry storms: cap attempts (say 5), back off exponentially with jitter, then dead-letter (a parking queue for messages that keep failing, inspected by humans) — infinite retries against a failing provider is self-inflicted DDoS. Quiet hours and per-user caps (max N marketing/day) are enforced at API time, not worker time, so suppressed messages never occupy queue capacity.

FOLLOW-UPS THEY WILL ASK: how do you batch digests ("5 people liked your post" instead of 5 pushes — aggregate in a short-window buffer keyed by user+type before enqueueing); how do you track opens/clicks (tracking pixel and wrapped links feeding the status store); what if Kafka itself is down (producers fall back to writing the request to a local durable log replayed later — never drop silently, never block the calling service); how do you test a 10M campaign safely (shadow send to a sink provider, sample real sends, ramp 1% → 10% → 100%).

sections.title: 8. Distributed Job Scheduler: Leases, SKIP LOCKED, and Time
sections.content:
A job scheduler ("run this at 9:00", "retry this payment in an hour", "every night at 2:00 rebuild the index") sounds like cron, and the interviewer picks it because the single-machine version is one line of crontab while the distributed version forces you through leases, idempotency, and clock trust — the core vocabulary of distributed coordination. The question underneath is always: how do you make MANY workers execute each job exactly once-ish, even while workers crash?

REQUIREMENTS. Functional: one-shot jobs (run at time T with payload), recurring jobs (cron expressions), retries with backoff, priorities, and status visibility (pending / running / succeeded / failed / dead). Non-functional: 10M scheduled jobs outstanding, 1,000 job executions/s at peak; a job fires within a few seconds of its due time; at-least-once execution (a job may rarely run twice, must never be silently skipped); no two workers run the same job concurrently in normal operation.

ESTIMATES. 10M jobs × ~1 KB = 10 GB of state — tiny. 1,000 claims/s of coordination traffic — modest. Say this explicitly: the scheduler is NOT a big-data problem; it is a CORRECTNESS problem, and a single well-indexed Postgres can be its heart for a long time. Interviewers reward candidates who resist reaching for exotic infrastructure when the numbers do not demand it.

DATA MODEL. jobs(id, run_at, priority, status, payload, attempts, max_attempts, lease_until, owner); index on (status, run_at). Recurring jobs live in a separate definitions table (id, cron_expr, next_run_at); each firing materializes a one-shot row, and the NEXT occurrence is scheduled when the current one completes — computing next-from-now rather than next-from-schedule is a policy choice (see misfires below).

THE CRUX: CLAIMING WITHOUT COLLISIONS. Naive workers all run SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE run_at <= now() AND status='pending' LIMIT 10 and then update the rows — two workers read the same rows in the gap between select and update, and both run the job. That is a race condition. The relational fix is one atomic claim:

```
 UPDATE jobs SET status='running', owner=:me,
        lease_until = now() + interval '30 seconds'
 WHERE id IN (
    SELECT id FROM jobs
    WHERE status='pending' AND run_at <= now()
    ORDER BY priority, run_at
    LIMIT 10
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED )
 RETURNING *;
```

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED tells the database: lock the rows you grab, and SKIP rows another worker already locked instead of waiting. Concurrent workers therefore claim disjoint jobs in one round trip, with zero external coordinator. This idiom is the single highest-value thing to know cold in this interview.

LEASES, NOT LOCKS. A worker that claims a job and dies would strand it forever under a plain lock. Hence lease_until: ownership that EXPIRES. The worker heartbeats (extends the lease) while running; a reaper process resets jobs whose lease expired back to pending, incrementing attempts. Consequence you must say unprompted: a worker that stalls (GC pause, network partition) past its lease looks dead, the job reruns, and the stalled worker may ALSO finish — so at-least-once is the honest guarantee and every job handler must be idempotent (safe to run twice: "set order.status=shipped" is; "send shipping email" needs a dedupe key, exactly as in the notification system).

```
 definitions --(materialize next firing)--> jobs table (Postgres)
                                               ^        |
                                    reaper: expire      | claim batch
                                    stale leases        v  (SKIP LOCKED)
                                               workers x N --> run handler
                                               | success: status=succeeded;
                                               | fail: attempts+1, backoff,
                                               |   re-pending; max -> dead
```

DEEP DIVE the interviewer will pick: TIME. Whose clock decides a job is due? If each worker uses its own wall clock, clock skew between workers reorders and double-fires jobs — so all due-ness comparisons use the DATABASE's now(), one authoritative clock. Second time problem: the top of the hour. Humans schedule everything at :00, so 50k jobs go due in the same second while your fleet does 1,000/s — a self-inflicted thundering herd. Fixes: add per-job random jitter (run_at + rand(0-60 s)) where the product allows, and let the queue drain by priority where it does not. Third: misfires — the scheduler was down from 1:55 to 2:30 and a 2:00 nightly job never fired. Policy per job, not global: run-once-now (catch up, single execution), skip (the 3:00 run covers it), or run-all-missed (billing jobs where every occurrence matters). Naming the three policies is the senior answer; picking one silently is the junior one.

BOTTLENECKS AND EVOLUTION. The jobs table becomes the contention point around ~10k claims/s: first shard it by hash(job_id) into N tables/databases with workers assigned to shards, or move the due-soon horizon (next hour) into Redis sorted sets (ZRANGEBYSCORE by run_at) with the DB as durable source of truth. Long-running jobs conflict with short leases — either heartbeat, or split the job into checkpointed stages so a retry resumes rather than restarts. Priorities can starve low-priority jobs under sustained load: reserve a worker slice for the lowest class.

FOLLOW-UPS THEY WILL ASK: why not cron on one box (single point of failure, no retries, no visibility, no horizontal scale — but SAY that below a few hundred jobs it is the right answer); why not Kafka as the job queue (Kafka delivers in log order and has no native "deliver at time T" — delay queues bolted on top are clumsy; a time-indexed store is the natural fit); how do you support job DAGs (jobs declare dependencies, a job becomes pending when all parents succeed — you have reinvented Airflow, and saying so shows you know the landscape); what stops the reaper from double-resetting (reaper updates are conditional: WHERE status='running' AND lease_until < now(), atomic per row).

sections.title: 9. Uber-lite: Geo-Indexing and Matching
sections.content:
Ride-hailing introduces a data shape none of the previous cases had: a continuous, high-frequency stream of GPS coordinates, and queries of the form "who is NEAR this point right now." The interviewer is testing whether you know why normal database indexes fail at proximity queries, one geo-indexing scheme in real detail, and how to run a match (an auction between one rider and several drivers) without dispatching the same driver twice.

REQUIREMENTS. Functional: drivers stream live location; riders request a ride and see nearby cars; the system matches a rider to the best available driver; both parties track the trip live. Non-functional: 500k drivers online at peak, each sending a location ping every 4 seconds; 1M ride requests/hour at peak; matching completes in under ~10 seconds; location data may be a few seconds stale (say this — it kills any temptation to make location writes durable); trip state (requested / matched / in-ride / completed) must NOT be lost, because money follows it.

ESTIMATES. Location writes: 500k / 4 s = 125,000 writes/s. At ~50 bytes a ping that is ~6 MB/s — bandwidth is nothing, but 125k QPS of writes rules out any durable disk-backed database on the hot path, and the data is worthless minutes later anyway. Conclusion: live locations live in MEMORY (sharded Redis or in-process state), with the ping stream teed to Kafka → S3 for offline analytics off the hot path. Matches: 1M/hour ≈ 280/s — small; matching is latency-sensitive, not throughput-heavy. The two workloads have opposite shapes, and splitting them is the design.

WHY B-TREES CANNOT DO "NEARBY". WHERE lat BETWEEN a AND b AND lng BETWEEN c AND d uses a B-tree on ONE column, then filters the other — an index on lat narrows to a horizontal stripe of the whole planet and scans it. Proximity needs a spatial index: a scheme that maps 2D space to keys such that near-in-space means near-in-keyspace. Three standard options: geohash (interleave the bits of lat and lng, encode base32 — longer shared prefix ≈ closer, roughly), quadtree (recursively split the map into 4 quadrants until each leaf holds few points — adapts to density), and hex grids like Uber's H3 (hexagons have uniform neighbor distances, which squares lack). For the interview, geohash is the easiest to wield: a 6-character geohash names a cell about 1.2 km × 0.6 km. Index drivers in Redis keyed by cell: SET geo:{cell6} -> {driver_id: lat,lng,heading,updated_at}; a ping moves the driver between cell sets. One caveat you must volunteer: prefix similarity breaks at cell boundaries (two points a street apart can be in cells with very different hashes), so a nearby query ALWAYS fetches the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbors — never the one cell alone.

```
 driver app --ping/4s--> location gw --> geo shards (Redis, by city+cell)
                                   \--> Kafka --> S3 (analytics, ETAs)
 rider app --request--> match svc --> query cell + 8 neighbors
                                  --> filter (available, car type)
                                  --> rank by road-ETA (routing svc)
                                  --> offer to driver #1 (15 s TTL)
                                  --> decline/timeout: driver #2 ...
                                  --> accept: trip svc (durable DB)
                                  --> push both apps via WebSocket
```

SHARDING: by city first (Mumbai and São Paulo never share queries — cities are natural, isolated partitions), by cell ranges within a city as load requires.

DEEP DIVE the interviewer will pick: THE MATCH ITSELF. Candidate drivers come back from the geo query; rank not by straight-line distance but by estimated road time (a river between you and a driver makes 300 m into 15 minutes — the routing/ETA service exists for this). Then the offer: send to the best driver with a 15-second window. Between offer and answer, that driver must not be offered another rider — this is a distributed locking problem, solved the lightweight way: a driver state machine (available → offered → on_trip) where the transition available→offered is atomic (Redis Lua compare-and-set, or a conditional DB update); a second match attempt on that driver fails the transition and takes its next candidate. Timeouts release the state back to available. Locking rider-side instead deadlocks nothing but wastes candidates; locking driver-side matches the scarce resource. Escalation when no driver accepts: widen the search ring, raise the price, or queue the rider — product policy, name all three.

Trip state, unlike location, is money: it goes in a durable relational store with an explicit state machine, and every transition is an audited row. Location can lie; the trip record cannot.

BOTTLENECKS AND EVOLUTION. Hot cells: a stadium empties and one cell holds 5,000 drivers and 20,000 open requests — fixed-size cells are the weakness of plain geohash (a quadtree or H3's multiple resolutions subdivide hot areas; with geohash you switch that region to 7-char cells). Reconnect storms after a network blip mirror the chat case: jittered backoff. Surge pricing is a per-cell supply/demand ratio computed from this same index every few seconds — a freebie answer when they ask "what else does this index give you?" GPS spoofing (fake drivers "appearing" near surge) needs plausibility checks: speed between pings, route continuity.

FOLLOW-UPS THEY WILL ASK: how are ETAs computed (contraction hierarchies over the road graph precomputed offline, adjusted by live traffic from the very pings you are collecting); what happens if the matched driver's app dies mid-offer (offer TTL expires, state machine releases, cascade continues — the design already answers it, point that out); how would you show live "cars near you" on the rider's map before any request (same 9-cell query, sampled and pushed at low frequency — do not burn matching capacity on eye candy); where do WebSockets come back (trip tracking pushes both parties' positions, reusing the chat-style gateway + session registry pattern).

sections.title: 10. YouTube-lite: Upload Pipeline, Transcoding, Serving
sections.content:
Video is the case where the two halves of the system have almost nothing in common: the upload/processing side is a heavy asynchronous batch pipeline measured in CPU-hours, and the watching side is a global content-delivery problem measured in terabits per second. The interviewer is testing whether you keep those halves separate, whether you know why video must be transcoded at all, and whether your bandwidth math shows you understand that the CDN IS the product.

REQUIREMENTS. Functional: upload videos up to 10 GB; process them into multiple qualities; stream globally with adaptive quality (playback should downshift on a bad connection instead of buffering); thumbnails; view counts. Non-functional: 1M uploads/day averaging 300 MB raw; 1B watch-sessions/day; time-to-playable after upload under ~10 minutes for a typical video; playback start under 2 seconds; durability — a creator's uploaded master must never be lost.

ESTIMATES — do these out loud, they carry the design. Ingest: 1M × 300 MB = 300 TB/day ≈ 3.5 GB/s sustained into storage. Transcode: a 10-minute 1080p video into a 5-rendition ladder at very roughly 2x realtime of CPU per rendition ≈ 100 core-minutes per video; × 1M/day = 100M core-minutes/day ÷ 1,440 ≈ 70,000 CPU cores running continuously. That number is why transcoding is a massive elastic worker fleet and why per-segment parallelism (below) exists. Egress: 1B views × ~5 minutes watched at ~3 Mbps ≈ 112 MB/view → ~112 PB/day ≈ 1.3 TB/s ≈ 10+ Tbps sustained. No origin datacenter serves that; 90%+ must come from CDN edge caches, and since a small fraction of videos gets most views, it can.

UPLOAD PATH. The client must not stream 10 GB through your API servers — they would become expensive proxies. Instead the API returns a presigned URL (a time-limited URL that lets the client PUT directly into blob storage such as S3, with the app server never touching the bytes). Uploads are chunked and resumable: the client uploads ~10 MB parts, each retryable, so a dropped mobile connection at 9.8 GB resumes at the last part instead of restarting. On completion, storage emits an event onto a queue and the pipeline wakes up.

```
 upload:  client --(1) POST /videos {meta} --> API -> metadata DB (status:
          uploading) + presigned part URLs
          client --(2) PUT parts --> blob store (raw masters bucket)
          --(3) complete event --> queue --> transcoding pipeline (DAG):
             probe -> split into ~10 s segments
                   -> encode each segment x each rendition (parallel fleet)
                   -> stitch/manifest per rendition -> thumbnails, captions
                   -> renditions bucket -> metadata DB (status: ready)

 watch:   player -> API: GET /videos/{id} -> manifest URL
          player -> CDN: manifest, then segments (cache miss -> origin bucket)
```

TRANSCODING DEEP DIVE — the interviewer will pick this. Why transcode at all: the uploaded master is one codec at one resolution; viewers span 240p phones on 2G and 4K TVs, so you produce a ladder of renditions (240p/360p/480p/720p/1080p...) at different bitrates. Why segments: encoding a 2-hour video serially takes hours of wall-clock; split it into ~10-second segments and encode hundreds of segments in parallel across the fleet, and wall-clock time collapses to roughly the longest segment plus stitching — this is how "under 10 minutes to playable" survives big files. It also gives cheap retries (re-encode one failed segment, not the movie) — the pipeline is a DAG of small idempotent steps, exactly the scheduler pattern from case 8. Codec economics is the senior flourish: AV1 compresses ~30% better than H.264 but costs an order of magnitude more CPU to encode — so encode everything in cheap H.264, and re-encode only proven-popular videos into AV1, where the one-time CPU cost is repaid by bandwidth savings across millions of views. Spending by view count, not uniformly, is the point.

SERVING. Adaptive streaming (HLS or DASH): each rendition is a list of small segment files plus a manifest describing them; the player measures its own throughput and requests the next segment from whichever rendition fits — quality shifts mid-stream with no server involvement. Segments are static immutable files, which is precisely what CDNs cache best. Unpopular long-tail videos miss the edge cache and pull from the origin bucket — slower start, acceptable; popular videos are pinned at edges worldwide.

DATA MODEL. Video metadata (id, owner, title, status, rendition manifest pointers) in a relational DB — small, transactional, fine. The bytes live in blob storage in two buckets: raw masters (never deleted, cold storage class after processing) and renditions (regenerable — deletable to save cost, at the price of re-transcoding). View counts are a hot-row problem: 100k concurrent viewers incrementing one counter row serializes on that row's lock — use sharded counters (N sub-rows per video, increment a random one, sum on read) or buffer increments in Redis and flush batched totals; and note that view counts can be approximate for display but must eventually reconcile for creator payments.

BOTTLENECKS AND EVOLUTION. A viral event floods uploads and the transcode queue backlogs: autoscale workers, and add priority lanes — a big creator's upload transcodes before a zero-subscriber upload; produce the 360p rendition FIRST so the video is playable early while the rest of the ladder fills in. Storage grows 100+ PB/year: tier cold, unwatched renditions to cheaper storage or drop them and re-encode on demand. Copyright/abuse scanning runs as an async pipeline stage — it must not block time-to-playable, but can unpublish after the fact.

FOLLOW-UPS THEY WILL ASK: how is live streaming different (ingest via RTMP/WebRTC, encode in real time with a strict latency budget, segments published as produced, no lookahead — a much harder pipeline with the same serving shape); where do recommendations fit (a separate ML system consuming view events from this pipeline's logs — descope it explicitly); DRM (encrypted segments, license server issues keys — mention, do not design); why 302-redirect players to CDN URLs rather than proxy (never move bytes through app servers — the rule from the upload path, applied twice).

sections.title: 11. The Building Blocks: What Each Buys You, and When It Is Wrong
sections.content:
Every case above assembles the same eight components. Interviewers notice whether you deploy them because you understand what each buys — and each one's failure mode — or because "that is what the diagrams on YouTube look like." This section is the honest spec sheet, one paragraph each: the problem it solves, the price you pay, and the misuse that makes an interviewer wince.

LOAD BALANCER: spreads requests across stateless replicas and hides instance deaths behind health checks (evict a dead backend in seconds). Price: it must be redundant itself (a single LB is a single point of failure — real deployments use pairs plus DNS). Misuse: balancing STATEFUL servers with naive round-robin — chat gateways holding sockets, or servers with session memory, need sticky routing or an external session registry; the moment state lives on a specific box, "any box will do" is false.

CACHE (Redis/Memcached): converts a ~10 ms disk-backed read into a ~0.5 ms memory read and absorbs read amplification (URL shortener: 100:1). Price: invalidation — cached data goes stale the moment the source changes, so every cache needs a stated policy (TTL, or explicit invalidation on write) and a stated tolerance ("feed may lag 1 minute"). Misuses: caching heavily-written data (invalidations churn faster than hits accrue — below ~10:1 read:write a cache mostly adds complexity); treating a cache as a database (Redis CAN persist, but if losing the dataset hurts, it needed a database's durability guarantees); ignoring stampedes — when a hot key expires, a thousand concurrent misses hit the DB at once (fix: per-key singleflight locks or staggered TTLs).

CDN: moves static bytes to edge servers near users, cutting the ~150 ms ocean round trip and offloading egress (YouTube's 10 Tbps). Price: invalidation lag and cost per GB. Misuse: putting personalized or rapidly-changing responses on it; a CDN caches by URL, so it shines exactly when one URL means the same immutable bytes for everyone — video segments, images, JS bundles — and fails when it does not.

MESSAGE QUEUE (Kafka/RabbitMQ/SQS): decouples producer speed from consumer speed, absorbs bursts, and makes retries a consumer-side concern (notifications, feed fan-out). Price: asynchrony — the caller no longer knows the work finished, so you need status tracking; plus at-least-once delivery means every consumer must be idempotent. Misuses: putting a queue where the caller NEEDS the answer (a rider cannot be "eventually matched" while staring at the screen — request/response paths stay synchronous); using Kafka as a scheduler (no deliver-at-time semantics, case 8); letting a queue hide a permanently under-provisioned consumer — a queue that only ever grows is an outage in progress with extra steps, which is why queue depth is the first metric to alarm on.

RELATIONAL DB (Postgres/MySQL): transactions (multi-row changes commit or vanish atomically), joins, secondary indexes, constraints the database enforces for you. Price: single-node write ceilings around low tens of thousands of writes/s, and sharding it yourself forfeits cross-shard joins and transactions. Misuse: reflexively declaring "SQL doesn't scale" — read replicas plus caching carry read-heavy products very far, and trip records, payments, and metadata BELONG here; equally wrong is forcing a 125k-writes/s ephemeral location stream (case 9) into it.

KEY-VALUE / WIDE-COLUMN STORE (DynamoDB/Cassandra): horizontal write scaling and predictable single-digit-ms reads, in exchange for querying ONLY by the key you designed around. Price: no joins, no ad-hoc queries — access patterns must be known up front, and new ones often mean new tables duplicating the data. Misuse: choosing it before knowing the access patterns; the flexibility you gave up is exactly what an early-stage product needs most.

BLOB STORE (S3/GCS): effectively infinite bytes, eleven nines of durability, per-object access; the only sane home for video masters, images, and backups. Price: latency (tens to hundreds of ms) and no queries over content. Misuse: streaming bytes THROUGH your app servers instead of presigned direct access (case 10) — app servers should broker permissions, not bandwidth.

SEARCH INDEX (Elasticsearch): inverted indexes (term → documents containing it) make text search and faceting fast where SQL LIKE '%term%' cannot use an index at all. Price: it is a REPLICA of truth, fed asynchronously from the primary store, so it is always slightly stale and can diverge — never the system of record. Misuse: using it as the primary database because "it also stores JSON."

The meta-skill the interviewer is watching for: every component you add is state to keep consistent, a failure mode to handle, and an on-call page to own. Strong candidates add a box only when a number demands it, and can say which number.

interviewQA.q: SQL or NoSQL for a given feature — how do you actually decide?
interviewQA.a: Decide from three questions, in order. First, access patterns: do you know exactly how the data will be queried? A URL shortener reads one row by exact key forever — key-value shaped. A young product with evolving queries needs SQL's ad-hoc flexibility (joins, secondary indexes), and choosing NoSQL early locks you into access patterns you have not discovered yet. Second, invariants: does correctness require multi-row atomicity — orders plus payments plus inventory moving together? That is transactions, which relational databases give you and most NoSQL stores restrict to a single item or partition. Third, write volume and shape: sustained writes beyond a single node's ceiling (tens of thousands per second) with simple key-based access — chat history at 70k msgs/s, time-series — is where Cassandra/DynamoDB genuinely earn their cost. The strong-candidate framing: 'SQL until a number forces otherwise, and here is the number.' Also name the hybrid reality: most real systems use both — trip records in Postgres, live locations in Redis, history in Cassandra — divided by workload, not ideology.
followUps: Your Postgres write master is at 80% CPU — walk through your options before reaching for Cassandra.
The interviewer says 'joins don't scale' — how do you respond precisely?
When would you pick a wide-column store even though your data fits comfortably in Postgres?

interviewQA.q: When is a message queue the wrong answer?
interviewQA.a: Three cases. First, when the caller needs the result to respond: a rider waiting for a match, a user waiting for a search — inserting a queue turns a request/response into 'eventually, maybe,' and now you need polling or callbacks to un-break the flow you broke. Synchronous paths should stay synchronous and scale with replicas. Second, when it hides an under-provisioned consumer: if consumers are permanently slower than producers, the queue grows without bound and you have converted an immediate, visible failure into a delayed, invisible one — queue depth is the first metric to alarm on precisely because of this. Third, when you need delivery at a specific time or strict global ordering: Kafka delivers in log order per partition as fast as consumers read; 'run this at 9 AM Tuesday' needs a time-indexed scheduler, not a queue. And every queue purchase includes at-least-once delivery, so all consumers must be idempotent — if the team cannot build idempotent handlers, the queue will manufacture duplicate emails and double-charged cards.
followUps: A teammate proposes a queue between the API and the database 'for reliability' — critique that.
How do you monitor a queue-based pipeline so backlog is caught before users notice?
When is a queue with a synchronous wait-for-reply pattern (RPC over queue) legitimate?

interviewQA.q: Push or pull fan-out for a social product — how do you choose, and where is the line?
interviewQA.a: Choose by comparing amplified cost on each side. Push (fan-out on write) pays follower-count writes per post and makes reads a single list fetch; pull (fan-out on read) pays followee-count reads per feed load and makes writes a single insert. Compute both: with 10M posts/day at 200 median followers, push costs ~23k inserts/s — cheap; with 2B feed loads/day at 200 followees, pull costs ~4.6M reads/s — brutal. In a read-heavy system push wins by the read:write ratio, EXCEPT where one author's follower count makes a single post's fan-out exceed your freshness budget: at 100k inserts/s of fleet capacity, a 100M-follower celebrity post takes ~17 minutes. So the line is computable: accounts whose follower count implies unacceptable fan-out lag flip to pull, and reads merge the precomputed list with live-fetched celebrity posts, which cache perfectly because millions of readers want the same few keys. Also push nothing to users inactive 30+ days — often half the fan-out volume for zero value.
followUps: Where exactly does read-your-writes consistency break in the hybrid, and how do you patch it?
How does the picture change for a group-messaging product versus a follower feed?
What operational metric tells you your celebrity threshold is set wrong?

interviewQA.q: Can you guarantee exactly-once delivery? What do you build instead?
interviewQA.a: Over a network, no — and saying so confidently is the point. If a worker sends an SMS and crashes before recording success, recovery must either resend (possible duplicate) or not (possible loss); the ambiguity is physics, not engineering. What you build is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing: retry until acknowledged, attach an idempotency key (a caller-generated unique ID per logical operation), and have the receiver deduplicate on it — claim the key atomically (Redis SETNX with TTL, or a unique constraint) before side-effecting. The user-visible result is indistinguishable from exactly-once. The judgment layer is choosing which failure you prefer per traffic class: claim-before-send converts duplicates into possible delay (right for marketing, billing); claim-after-send risks duplicates but never loss (right for OTP, where a second SMS is harmless and a missing one is a support ticket). Kafka's 'exactly-once semantics' deserves one sentence: it is transactional exactly-once processing within the Kafka ecosystem, not exactly-once delivery to external systems like a phone.
followUps: What TTL do you put on dedupe keys and what breaks at each extreme?
How does this interact with a job scheduler's lease expiry rerunning a handler?
Design the idempotency story for a payment capture endpoint specifically.

interviewQA.q: How do you choose a shard key, and what are the classic mistakes?
interviewQA.a: A shard key must do two jobs: spread load evenly, and keep each frequent query on ONE shard. Start from the top queries, not from the data. Chat shards by conversation_id — every 'latest messages in this chat' is shard-local, and one owner per conversation gives free ordering. The URL shortener shards by code — random, so uniform, and every read names its shard. Classic mistakes: sharding by a low-cardinality or skewed key (shard-by-country puts India and Iceland on equal hardware); sharding by time (all of today's writes hammer the newest shard while old shards idle — fine for archival reads, terrible for write spreading); sharding by a key your queries do not contain, making every read a scatter-gather across all shards; and forgetting that some access pattern always crosses shards — 'all messages by user X' fights the conversation sharding, so you either maintain a second index keyed the other way or accept a fan-out query. Say the resharding cost too: changing a shard key later means migrating live data, which is why consistent hashing (only 1/N of keys move when a node joins) exists.
followUps: Your chosen key develops one hot shard in production — enumerate your options in order of preference.
Why does auto-increment as a shard key cause problems, and what replaces it?
How does consistent hashing reduce resharding pain, and what problem do virtual nodes solve?

interviewQA.q: When do you add a cache, and what new problems have you signed up for?
interviewQA.a: Add a cache when a read-heavy ratio (10:1 or more), measurable latency need, or hot-spot concentration justifies it — the URL shortener's 100:1 redirect ratio, the feed's post-hydration path — and never for write-heavy data, where invalidation churn outpaces hits. The moment it is in, you own four new problems. Staleness: define per cache how stale is acceptable and enforce it with TTL or write-time invalidation; 'cache-aside with TTL' is the default answer (read: try cache, miss → DB → fill; write: update DB, delete key). Stampede: a hot key expires and a thousand concurrent misses hit the DB at once — fix with per-key singleflight locking or jittered TTLs. Hot keys: one celebrity's key can exceed a single cache node's capacity — replicate that key or layer a local in-process cache. Cold start: a restarted cache means a miss storm on the DB — warm it, or ramp traffic gradually. Also state the invalidation trap in dual-write form: 'update DB then update cache' races under concurrency; 'update DB then DELETE cache key' is safer because the next read repopulates from truth.
followUps: Why is delete-on-write safer than set-on-write, and what narrow race remains even then?
Your cache hit rate is 60% — is that good? What would you look at before deciding?
When is caching at the client or CDN layer strictly better than Redis in front of the DB?

interviewQA.q: WebSockets, long polling, or server-sent events — how do you choose?
interviewQA.a: Choose by direction and frequency of server-initiated data. WebSockets (a persistent bidirectional TCP connection upgraded from HTTP) win when both sides push frequently — chat, live trip tracking, multiplayer — because per-message overhead is bytes and latency is one hop. Their cost is statefulness: each connection pins a socket to one server, so you inherit session registries, sticky routing, heartbeats, and reconnect storms with jittered backoff. Server-sent events (a one-way HTTP stream from server to client) cover 'server pushes, client mostly listens' — live scores, notification badges — with plain HTTP semantics, automatic reconnect, and no upgrade dance; the client sends its rare messages over normal requests. Long polling (client parks a request until data or timeout, then re-requests) is the compatibility fallback — works through every proxy and firewall, but each message costs a full request cycle, and 12.5M clients re-polling every 2 seconds is millions of mostly-empty QPS, which is the arithmetic that justifies sockets in the chat case. Interview answer shape: name the traffic pattern first, then the mechanism, then the operational cost you accept.
followUps: A gateway holding 250k sockets dies — walk through the next 60 seconds of system behavior.
Why do WebSockets complicate load balancing, and what are the two standard fixes?
Where would plain periodic polling actually be the RIGHT answer?

interviewQA.q: One key gets 100x the traffic of everything else — what is your hot-key playbook?
interviewQA.a: First identify which layer melts: a hot cache key saturating one Redis node, a hot DB row serializing on its lock (view counters), a hot shard (celebrity's data), or a hot cell (airport surge in geo-indexing) — the fix differs by layer. For hot READS: replicate the key (store it on N cache nodes, read a random replica), add a local in-process cache on every app server so most reads never leave the box, and push truly universal content (viral video segments) to the CDN. For hot WRITES: shard the counter — split one logical counter into N sub-counters, increment a random one, sum on read — or buffer increments in memory and flush batches, accepting bounded staleness of the displayed value. For hot PARTITIONS: split the partition finer (geohash 6 → 7 at a stadium; a customer's rate-limit counter into K sub-counters summed approximately). The senior framing is that most hot-key fixes trade exactness for spread — sharded counters are eventually accurate, replicated caches are briefly inconsistent — so name the staleness you are accepting and why the product tolerates it.
followUps: How do you DETECT hot keys before they page you — what instrumentation exists?
Why does consistent hashing alone not save you from a hot key?
A single conversation in your chat app becomes a 500k-member broadcast channel — what redesign follows?

interviewQA.q: Strong or eventual consistency — how do you decide feature by feature?
interviewQA.a: Ask: what breaks if two observers briefly see different values? Money and invariants break — a seat sold twice, a balance overdrawn, a username registered twice — so payments, inventory decrements, and uniqueness claims need strong consistency (all readers see the write immediately, typically via a single-leader database and transactions). Human-facing counts and feeds do not break — a like count off by three for ten seconds, a feed missing the newest post for a minute — so they take eventual consistency (replicas converge after a delay) and buy availability and latency with it. Two refinements mark a strong candidate. First, read-your-writes as a middle tier: users tolerate OTHERS' staleness but not their own — after posting, your own feed must show the post — which you get by reading your own recent writes from the leader or unioning them in at read time, without paying for global strong consistency. Second, consistency is per-OPERATION, not per-system: the same product strongly-consistently charges the card and eventually-consistently updates the order-history page, and drawing that line feature by feature is exactly the skill being probed.
followUps: Where does read-your-writes come from mechanically in a leader-replica Postgres setup?
Give a concrete user story where eventual consistency in a shopping cart is acceptable and one where it is not.
How does the celebrity-feed hybrid interact with consistency expectations?

interviewQA.q: Redis as the primary datastore — when is that acceptable?
interviewQA.a: Acceptable when the data is ephemeral, reconstructible, or tolerably lossy — and you can say which. Live driver locations regenerate every 4 seconds; rate-limiter counters reset by design; session tokens force a re-login at worst; a feed cache rebuilds from the posts table. In all of these, losing the Redis dataset costs seconds of degradation, so Redis's persistence model (snapshots plus an append-only file that can still lose the last moments on crash, and async replication that can lose acknowledged writes on failover) is a fine trade for sub-millisecond reads at 100k+ ops/s. Unacceptable when loss means corruption of truth: orders, messages users expect to keep, anything billing-adjacent — the chat design writes to Cassandra BEFORE delivering precisely so the socket layer and its registries can be lossy. The interview trap is 'Redis has AOF persistence, so it is durable' — fsync-every-write kills its performance advantage, and failover can still discard acknowledged writes; if you find yourself hardening Redis into a database, the requirement was a database. State it as: Redis is where I put data I can afford to lose, and here is why THIS data qualifies.
followUps: What actually happens to acknowledged writes during a Redis primary failover?
Your feed cache lost everything at peak — describe the recovery path and its DB impact.
When would you choose Redis Cluster versus client-side sharding across independent instances?

interviewQA.q: How do you make a write endpoint idempotent in practice?
interviewQA.a: Idempotent means calling it twice has the same effect as once — mandatory wherever retries exist, which is everywhere (client timeouts, queue redelivery, lease expiry). Techniques in order of preference. Natural idempotency: writes that SET state rather than APPLY deltas — 'status = shipped' is repeat-safe, 'balance += 100' never is; where possible, reshape mutations into absolute assignments. Idempotency keys: the CALLER generates a unique ID per logical operation (client message UUID, event_id+user+channel), the server records it with a unique constraint or atomic SETNX, and a duplicate arrival returns the ORIGINAL response rather than re-executing — Stripe's API is the canonical example to name. Conditional writes: compare-and-set ('UPDATE ... WHERE status = pending') makes replays no-ops because the precondition fails on the second run; this is also how the job scheduler's reaper and the driver state machine avoid double transitions. The two implementation details interviewers probe: dedupe records need retention policy (a TTL shorter than your longest possible retry window reopens the duplicate hole), and the key must cover the LOGICAL operation, not the HTTP attempt — a client retry must reuse the same key or the whole scheme is decorative.
followUps: Why must the idempotency key be generated by the client rather than the server?
How do you make 'increment view count' effectively idempotent, or do you not bother — and why?
Where should the dedupe check live when the endpoint fans out to three downstream services?

interviewQA.q: What belongs on a CDN, and what breaks when you put the wrong thing there?
interviewQA.a: A CDN caches responses BY URL at edge servers near users. It belongs in front of content where one URL means the same bytes for every viewer for a while: video segments, images, JS/CSS bundles, and — the underrated one — hot API responses that are identical across users, like the top-10 suggestions for 1-2 character typeahead prefixes or a public trending list with a 60-second TTL. The wins are the ~150 ms cross-ocean round trip removed and origin egress collapsed — YouTube-lite's 10+ Tbps is unservable from origin at all. What breaks with the wrong content: personalized responses cached at the edge leak one user's data to another (the classic Vary-header/cookie misconfiguration incident); rapidly-changing data serves stale versions for the TTL window with no read-your-writes; and anything requiring auth decisions per request cannot be judged by an edge that only sees the URL (signed URLs with expiry are the standard patch — the origin brokers permission, the edge serves bytes). Rule of thumb to state: the more immutable and universal the bytes, the closer to the user they should live; versioned immutable URLs (bundle.a1b2c3.js) plus infinite TTL is the endgame of that logic.
followUps: How do you invalidate a CDN-cached object NOW, and why do versioned URLs make that a non-event?
Design the caching headers for video segments versus the video's metadata JSON.
What is origin shield / request coalescing, and which thundering-herd problem does it solve?

interviewQA.q: How do you shard a relational database, and what do you give up?
interviewQA.a: Shard when a single writer node genuinely cannot carry the write load or working set — AFTER read replicas, caching, and bigger hardware are exhausted, because sharding is the point of no return for schema flexibility. Mechanics: pick a shard key from your top queries (see the shard-key question), route in the application or a proxy layer (Vitess, Citus), and use consistent hashing or a directory service so adding shards moves 1/N of data, not all of it. What you give up, concretely: cross-shard JOINs (now application-side merges or denormalized copies); cross-shard TRANSACTIONS (moving money between users on different shards now needs two-phase commit or, realistically, a saga — a sequence of local transactions with compensating rollbacks); global UNIQUE constraints and auto-increment (replaced by Snowflake-style IDs: timestamp + machine + sequence, which also sort by time); and painless ad-hoc analytics (now a warehouse fed by change-data-capture). The strong answer names the alternative first: 'at this write volume I would first do X and Y; sharding starts when the number reaches Z' — reaching for sharding early signals inexperience as loudly as never reaching for it.
followUps: Walk through resharding 8 shards to 16 with zero downtime.
What is a saga, and how does it replace the cross-shard transaction you lost?
Why do Snowflake IDs beat UUIDv4 as primary keys in a sharded SQL store?

interviewQA.q: A critical dependency is down — do you fail open or fail closed, and who decides?
interviewQA.a: Fail-open means proceeding without the dependency's answer; fail-closed means refusing to proceed. Decide by comparing the cost of the two wrong outcomes, per call site — never globally. Rate limiter down: fail-open for product endpoints (an internal outage must not become a customer outage; the limiter protects capacity, and brief unprotection is survivable) but fail-closed for login, OTP, and password reset (unlimited attempts during an outage is a free brute-force window — the limiter there is a security control, and security controls fail closed). Fraud check down: fail-open under a dollar threshold, closed above it — encode the risk tolerance as a number. Feature flags/config service down: fail to last-known-good values cached locally, which is a third option worth naming — degrade to stale rather than to open or closed. The decision belongs to the OWNER of the harmed party's risk (security team for auth, product for checkout), made in design review and encoded in config — not improvised by whoever is on call at 3 AM. In the interview, volunteering the split — 'open here, closed there, and here is the asymmetry of harm' — is precisely the judgment the question exists to sample.
followUps: How does a circuit breaker interact with the fail-open/closed decision?
What monitoring distinguishes 'failing open by design' from 'silently broken'?
Give a case where fail-open on a security control is nonetheless correct.

interviewQA.q: Kafka or RabbitMQ — what is the real difference and when does each win?
interviewQA.a: They implement different abstractions. Kafka is a replicated append-only LOG: producers append to partitioned topics, messages persist for a retention window regardless of consumption, and each consumer group tracks its own offset — so multiple independent consumers replay the same stream, ordering is guaranteed per partition, and throughput reaches millions of messages/s. RabbitMQ is a smart BROKER: it routes each message to queues, delivers to a worker, and deletes on acknowledgment — richer routing (topic exchanges, per-message TTLs, priorities, dead-lettering built in) and lower per-message latency, but a consumed message is gone and total throughput is an order of magnitude lower. Kafka wins for event streams feeding MULTIPLE consumers (view events consumed by the counter service, the recommender, and the warehouse independently), replay after a bug ('reprocess yesterday'), and firehose volumes like the driver-location tee. RabbitMQ wins for classic task distribution — the notification system's channel workers — where each message means one unit of work done once, and routing/priority semantics do real lifting. The trap answer is 'Kafka because scale'; the strong answer is 'how many independent readers, and do I ever replay?'
followUps: How do consumer groups and partition counts constrain your parallelism in Kafka?
Where do delayed/scheduled messages fit — which system handles them and how?
Your Kafka consumer lag is growing steadily — enumerate causes in likelihood order.

interviewQA.q: Why does OFFSET pagination break at scale, and what replaces it?
interviewQA.a: Two independent failures. Performance: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000 makes the database walk and discard 100,000 rows to return 20 — cost grows linearly with page depth, so deep pages and crawlers produce pathological load. Correctness: the feed shifts under the reader — if new rows arrive between page 1 and page 2, offsets now point 20 rows earlier, so the reader sees duplicates (or, on deletion, silently skips rows). The replacement is cursor (keyset) pagination: each page returns an opaque cursor encoding the last item's stable sort key — 'WHERE (created_at, id) < (cursor) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20' — which is an index seek (constant cost at any depth) and is immune to inserts above the cursor. Requirements to state: the sort key must be unique and immutable (hence the id tiebreaker — timestamps collide), which is one more reason Snowflake-style time-sortable IDs pervade feed systems; and cursors should be opaque tokens, not raw values, so clients cannot construct or tamper with them. Offset survives legitimately in small, jump-to-page-7 admin tables where depth is bounded and the data barely moves. Feed, chat history, and search-results pagination in every case study here is cursor-based.
followUps: How do you paginate a feed that is MERGED at read time from a pushed list plus pulled celebrity posts?
What goes inside the cursor token for a ranked (non-chronological) feed?
How do you handle a cursor that references a now-deleted item?

interviewQA.q: Show me your back-of-envelope method — estimate QPS and storage for a photo-sharing app in two minutes.
interviewQA.a: Fix round numbers, state them as assumptions, and keep every figure to one significant digit. Users: say 100M DAU. Behavior: each user views 50 photos and uploads 0.2/day. Day = 86,400 s ≈ 10^5. Reads: 100M × 50 = 5B/day ÷ 10^5 ≈ 50k QPS average; peak ×3 ≈ 150k. Writes: 100M × 0.2 = 20M/day ≈ 200 QPS — read:write is 250:1, so the architecture will be cache-and-CDN-shaped; say that conclusion immediately, because conclusions are what estimates are FOR. Storage: 20M photos/day × 2 MB average (after server-side compression) = 40 TB/day; times 365 ≈ 15 PB/year — so blob storage with tiering, and thumbnails (20 KB × several sizes) are negligible next to originals. Bandwidth: 150k views/s × 200 KB served size ≈ 30 GB/s ≈ 240 Gbps — CDN territory, origin cannot serve it. Metadata: 20M rows/day × 500 B = 10 GB/day — comfortably relational. The graded skills: rounding aggressively without apology, sanity-checking against knowns (does 15 PB/year sound like a photo product? yes), and ending each number with the design decision it forces rather than leaving it as trivia.
followUps: Which of those numbers would you actually verify first if this were a real project, and how?
Redo the egress estimate assuming 60% of views hit photos uploaded in the last 24 hours.
How does the design change if the read:write ratio were 5:1 instead of 250:1?

interviewQA.q: Your database, cache, and search index all hold copies of the same data — how do you keep them in sync?
interviewQA.a: Name the trap first: dual-writes — the application writing to DB and cache and Elasticsearch in sequence — fails partially (the write to the third succeeds after the second failed, or two concurrent updates land in different orders in different stores), and there is no transaction spanning heterogeneous systems, so the copies silently diverge. The robust pattern is a single source of truth plus derived replicas fed by its change stream: writes go ONLY to the primary database; change-data-capture (CDC — tailing the database's replication log, e.g. Debezium) publishes every committed change to Kafka; independent consumers update the cache, the search index, and the warehouse. Because the log is ordered and replayable, a crashed consumer resumes without loss, a corrupted index is rebuilt by replaying history, and adding a fifth replica later touches zero application code. The costs to state: replicas lag by the pipeline latency (typically sub-second to seconds — fine for search, needing care where users expect read-your-writes, which you patch by reading the primary for the writer's own data), and consumers must be idempotent because the log delivers at-least-once. For the cache specifically, the lazy alternative — cache-aside with delete-on-write and TTL as a backstop — is honest and adequate when only two stores exist; CDC earns its machinery when the third replica shows up.
followUps: Why is 'transactional outbox' the fallback when you cannot tail the database log, and how does it work?
A CDC consumer applied events out of order after a repartition — what invariant was violated and how do you prevent it?
How do you rebuild a 2 TB search index from the log without taking search down?

flashcards.front: Seconds in a day, and the shortcut for converting daily volume to QPS?
flashcards.back: 86,400 s ≈ 10^5. So 1M/day ≈ 12/s, 100M/day ≈ 1,200/s, 1B/day ≈ 12,000/s. Peak is 2-3x average for normal products, up to 10x for bursty ones (ticket sales, live events).

flashcards.front: Latency ladder: RAM read, SSD random read, disk seek, same-DC round trip, cross-ocean round trip?
flashcards.back: RAM ~100 ns; SSD random read ~100 µs; disk seek ~10 ms; round trip within a datacenter ~0.5 ms; cross-ocean round trip ~150 ms. RAM beats disk ~100x — the arithmetic behind every cache; the 150 ms is why CDNs exist.

flashcards.front: URL shortener: why are 7 base62 characters enough?
flashcards.back: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes. At 100M new URLs/month for 5 years you need 6 billion — 500x headroom. 6 chars (57B) would also fit but with little margin.

flashcards.front: 301 vs 302 redirect for a link shortener — which and why?
flashcards.back: 302 (temporary). A 301 is cached by the browser, so repeat clicks bypass your servers — you lose all analytics and cannot change or expire the mapping. 302 keeps every click on your servers; that traffic is the product.

flashcards.front: Three ways to generate short-URL codes, and the usual winner?
flashcards.back: Hash the URL (collisions, must reprobe); global counter → base62 (clean but single point of failure); counter with pre-allocated RANGES per server (winner — no collisions, no SPOF, a crashed server wastes one block). Caveat: sequential codes are guessable.

flashcards.front: Token bucket: what state per key, and what behavior does it allow that fixed windows do not?
flashcards.back: Two numbers: current tokens and last-refill time. Refill at rate r up to capacity c; each request spends a token. Allows bursts up to c while capping sustained rate at r — and avoids the fixed-window flaw of 2x bursts straddling a window boundary.

flashcards.front: Why does a Redis rate limiter need a Lua script?
flashcards.back: Read-check-write as separate commands is a race: two gateways both read 9 under limit 10 and both allow. Redis runs a Lua script atomically, so refill+compare+decrement happens with no interleaving. (Alternative: INCR-then-check the returned value.)

flashcards.front: Fail-open vs fail-closed: the rule of thumb when the rate limiter is down?
flashcards.back: Fail-open for product endpoints — an internal outage must not become a customer outage. Fail-closed for login/OTP/password-reset — otherwise the outage is a free brute-force window. Security controls fail closed; capacity controls fail open.

flashcards.front: Chat: why WebSockets instead of polling — what is the arithmetic?
flashcards.back: 12.5M concurrent clients polling every 2 s = ~6M QPS of mostly-empty responses. A WebSocket (persistent bidirectional TCP connection) delivers pushes instantly at bytes of overhead. Cost: state — session registry, heartbeats, reconnect storms.

flashcards.front: Chat: what is the session registry and why is it needed?
flashcards.back: A map user_id → gateway holding that user's socket (in Redis, written on connect, expired by heartbeat). With ~50 gateway boxes, the chat service must know WHERE the recipient's connection lives to deliver a push. Stale entry → delivery fails → fall back to push notification and repair.

flashcards.front: Why can't wall-clock timestamps order chat messages, and what does instead?
flashcards.back: Clock skew: servers' clocks disagree by milliseconds, so a reply can carry an earlier timestamp than its question. Fix: route each conversation to one owning shard that assigns a per-conversation monotonic sequence number — one writer makes ordering local and trivial.

flashcards.front: The formula that fakes exactly-once messaging?
flashcards.back: At-least-once transport (retry until ack) + idempotent receiver (dedupe on a client-generated message UUID) = looks exactly-once to users. True exactly-once delivery over a failing network is impossible — say so, then give this construction.

flashcards.front: News feed: cost of pure push vs pure pull at 200M DAU, 10M posts/day, 200 followers median?
flashcards.back: Push: 10M × 200 = 2B feed-list inserts/day ≈ 23k/s — cheap. Pull: 2B feed loads × 200 followee reads = 400B reads/day ≈ 4.6M/s — brutal. Read-heavy ⇒ push wins, except celebrities: 100M followers ≈ 17 min of fan-out for one post ⇒ they go pull.

flashcards.front: Feed hybrid: what happens at read time?
flashcards.back: Fetch the user's precomputed feed list (pushed), fetch recent posts of the few celebrities they follow (pulled, heavily shared cache), merge, hydrate post content from cache, rank. Own posts are inserted synchronously (read-your-writes).

flashcards.front: Cheapest 50% cost cut in feed fan-out?
flashcards.back: Skip followers inactive 30+ days — often half of fan-out volume delivers to accounts that never return. Rebuild a returning user's feed once via a pull-mode query. Also store only post IDs in feed lists (~300, capped) and hydrate at read.

flashcards.front: Typeahead: why is QPS a multiple of search volume?
flashcards.back: Every keystroke fires a request: 5B searches/day × ~4 keystrokes ≈ 20B req/day ≈ 230k/s average, ~500k/s peak. Mitigate with client debounce (~50 ms), client-side caching, and CDN caching of 1-2 character prefixes (the hottest, most static results).

flashcards.front: Typeahead: why precompute top-k at every trie node?
flashcards.back: Without it, a query must explore the whole subtree under the prefix and sort by frequency — thousands of nodes for short prefixes, dead at 500k QPS. With top-10 stored per node, a query is a prefix walk + one list read: microseconds. Build cost paid offline, bottom-up (merge children's lists).

flashcards.front: Pattern for updating a live in-memory index (trie, routing table) under heavy reads?
flashcards.back: Never mutate in place. Build a new versioned snapshot offline, load it alongside the old, atomically swap a pointer, discard the old. Freshness gap covered by a small frequently-rebuilt overlay merged at query time.

flashcards.front: Notification system: why separate queues for OTP and marketing?
flashcards.back: Isolation. A 10M-message campaign must not delay a login code that has a 5-second budget. Separate topics per channel AND priority, with dedicated workers for the critical lane — a shared queue lets bulk traffic starve urgent traffic. Classic interview probe.

flashcards.front: What is an idempotency key and who generates it?
flashcards.back: A unique ID per LOGICAL operation (not per HTTP attempt), generated by the CALLER, recorded by the server via unique constraint or atomic SETNX; duplicates return the original result instead of re-executing. Client-generated because only the caller knows a retry is the same operation.

flashcards.front: What is a dead-letter queue and why cap retries?
flashcards.back: A parking queue for messages that keep failing after N attempts (with exponential backoff + jitter), inspected by humans. Without a cap, retries against a failing dependency become a self-inflicted DDoS and poison-pill messages block the queue forever.

flashcards.front: The SQL idiom that lets many workers claim jobs without double-claiming?
flashcards.back: UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ... WHERE status='pending' AND run_at <= now() ORDER BY run_at LIMIT k FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING *. SKIP LOCKED makes concurrent workers skip rows others hold, so claims are disjoint, atomic, coordinator-free.

flashcards.front: Leases vs locks in a job scheduler — why leases, and what guarantee follows?
flashcards.back: A crashed worker holding a plain lock strands the job forever. A lease expires (lease_until), heartbeats extend it, a reaper re-pends expired jobs. But a stalled-not-dead worker may ALSO finish ⇒ the honest guarantee is at-least-once, so every handler must be idempotent.

flashcards.front: A scheduler was down when a job was due (misfire). What are the three policies?
flashcards.back: Run-once-now (catch up with a single execution), skip (next scheduled run covers it), run-all-missed (every occurrence matters, e.g. billing). Policy is per-job, chosen by the job owner — naming all three is the senior answer.

flashcards.front: Why can't a B-tree index answer 'drivers near me'?
flashcards.back: Nearby is a 2D predicate; a B-tree serves one column, so lat BETWEEN narrows to a horizontal stripe of the planet and scans it. Spatial schemes (geohash, quadtree, H3) map 2D to keys where near-in-space ≈ near-in-keyspace.

flashcards.front: Geohash query gotcha: why must you always fetch 9 cells?
flashcards.back: Prefix similarity breaks at cell boundaries — two points a street apart can land in cells with very different hashes. So a proximity query fetches the target cell PLUS its 8 neighbors, always. (6-char cell ≈ 1.2 km × 0.6 km.)

flashcards.front: Uber: where do live driver locations live, and why not in a durable DB?
flashcards.back: In memory (sharded Redis by city+cell): 500k drivers / 4 s = 125k writes/s of data that is worthless minutes later. Tee pings to Kafka → S3 for analytics off the hot path. Trip state, by contrast, is money: durable relational DB with an audited state machine.

flashcards.front: How does dispatch avoid offering one driver to two riders?
flashcards.back: Driver state machine available → offered → on_trip with an ATOMIC transition (Redis Lua compare-and-set or conditional UPDATE). The second match attempt fails the transition and cascades to the next candidate; offer TTL (~15 s) releases state on timeout.

flashcards.front: What is a presigned URL and which rule does it embody?
flashcards.back: A time-limited URL letting the client PUT/GET directly against blob storage, authorized in advance by your API. Embodies: app servers broker permissions, never bandwidth — 10 GB uploads and video serving must not stream through application servers.

flashcards.front: Why split videos into ~10 s segments before transcoding?
flashcards.back: Parallelism: hundreds of segments encode simultaneously across the fleet, so a 2-hour video's wall-clock ≈ longest segment + stitch, not hours. Also cheap retries (redo one segment) and it yields exactly the small immutable files HLS/DASH serving needs.

flashcards.front: What is adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH)?
flashcards.back: Each rendition (240p…4K) is a manifest + small segment files. The player measures its own throughput and requests the next segment from whichever rendition fits — quality shifts mid-stream with zero server logic. Immutable segments are ideal CDN objects.

flashcards.front: Hot row: 100k viewers incrementing one view-count row — fix?
flashcards.back: Sharded counters: N sub-rows per video, increment a random one, sum on read. Or buffer increments in Redis and flush batches. Display can be approximate; reconcile exactly later where money depends on it (creator payouts).

flashcards.front: Cache stampede: what is it and two fixes?
flashcards.back: A hot key expires and thousands of concurrent misses hit the DB at once. Fixes: per-key singleflight (one request rebuilds, others wait) and jittered/staggered TTLs so keys don't expire together. Related: warm caches before shifting traffic after restarts.

flashcards.front: Offset vs cursor pagination — the two failures of OFFSET?
flashcards.back: Cost: OFFSET 100000 walks and discards 100k rows — linear in depth. Correctness: inserts/deletes shift offsets between pages → duplicates or skips. Cursor/keyset (WHERE (created_at,id) < last-seen ORDER BY … LIMIT n) is an index seek, stable under inserts.

flashcards.front: Dual-write problem and the standard fix?
flashcards.back: App writing DB + cache + search index separately fails partially and diverges — no cross-system transaction exists. Fix: single source of truth; CDC (tail the DB's change log, e.g. Debezium) → Kafka → idempotent consumers update each replica. Replayable, ordered, rebuildable.

flashcards.front: Thundering herd: two places it appears in these cases and the shared cure?
flashcards.back: 250k chat clients reconnecting after a gateway dies; 50k cron jobs due at :00. Cure: jitter — randomized exponential backoff on reconnects, randomized offsets on schedules — plus gradual admission. Synchronized clients are self-inflicted DDoS.
